papers.summary: In cultured human breast cancer and embryonic stem cells, low oxygen shifted transcription start sites (where gene reading begins) alongside changes in the histone mark H3K4me3. Drugs altering H3K4me3 reproduced or reversed these shifts without low oxygen, independent of HIF-1 (the main low-oxygen sensor protein), and boosted synthesis of the metabolic enzyme PDK1.
papers.why_it_matters: Identifies in cultured human cells an epigenetic route to low-oxygen adaptation operating alongside, and partly independent of, the classic HIF-1 pathway.
papers.notes: In vitro cell-culture study in two human cell lines (T47D and H9); not yet tested in whole organisms.

papers.title: DESI DR2 results. II. Measurements of baryon acoustic oscillations and cosmological constraints
papers.authors: DESI Collaboration
papers.headline: DESI and other surveys hint that dark energy may change
papers.summary: DESI used more than 14 million galaxies and quasars, extremely bright galaxy centers, to measure a characteristic spacing left by early sound waves. Adding measurements of early-universe light and supernovae favored changing dark energy by 2.8 to 4.2 standard deviations, depending on which supernova sample was used.
papers.why_it_matters: The result gives astronomers a test of whether the cause of accelerating expansion is constant or changes with time.
papers.notes: DESI’s spacing measurements alone are well described by the standard flat model; its inferred values are 2.3 standard deviations from those inferred from early-universe light. The stronger preference comes from combining datasets.

papers.title: Human adaptation to high-altitude: A contemporary comparison of the oxygen cascade in Andean, Tibetan and Ethiopian highlanders
papers.authors: Ayechew A. Getu, Melissa Ilardo, Joshua C. Tremblay et al.
papers.headline: Andean, Tibetan and Ethiopian highlanders solved low oxygen in different ways
papers.summary: This physiological review compares each step of oxygen delivery, from breathing to muscle use, across three human highland populations. Tibetans show brisk breathing responses and efficient tissue blood flow, Andeans rely more on high hemoglobin with elevated lung-artery pressure, and Ethiopian Amhara maintain near sea-level breathing alongside high blood oxygen saturation.
papers.why_it_matters: Summarizes how millennia at high altitude produced distinct human physiological adaptations to the same low-oxygen challenge.
papers.notes: Narrative comparative review; the authors note physiological data on Ethiopian highlanders remain limited compared with Tibetans and Andeans.

papers.title: Psychological assessments, allostatic load and gene expression analyses in a randomized controlled trial comparing meditation, yoga, and stress education
papers.authors: John W. Denninger, Diane Joss, Perla M. Romero et al.
papers.headline: Controlled meditation and yoga trial found no gene-expression edge over stress education
papers.summary: In 211 chronically stressed but healthy adults randomized to eight weeks of meditation, yoga or stress education (~70 per group), all three groups improved on psychological questionnaires. No significant differences appeared between groups on physiological stress biomarkers or blood gene-expression measures at nine or 26 weeks.
papers.why_it_matters: Provides an important controlled human null result, showing mind-body practices did not outperform active stress education on blood gene expression.
papers.notes: Null between-group result in otherwise healthy stressed adults (NCT01308970); published in Frontiers in Psychology.

papers.title: Fundamental constants: from measurement to the universe, a window on gravitation and cosmology
papers.authors: Jean-Philippe Uzan
papers.headline: A review compares ways to test whether nature’s constants change
papers.summary: The review examines what atomic clocks, ancient natural reactors, distant galaxies’ light, and other evidence reveal about the stability of physical constants. It explains what each test measures and how its assumptions affect the limits it can place on possible variation in space or time.
papers.why_it_matters: These measurements help separate what experiments say about nature’s constants from speculation about why they have their values.

papers.title: Small but Still Significant: Awe and the Self
papers.authors: Megan E. Edwards, Katelyn Mendenhall, Christopher Sanders et al.
papers.headline: Awe can make people feel small without making them feel insignificant
papers.summary: Across four experiments, participants reported how large and how significant they felt before and after awe-inducing or comparison activities. Awe reduced how large they felt in a metaphorical sense, but did not reduce personal significance. Increases in perceived significance occurred across conditions and were not specific to awe.
papers.why_it_matters: It distinguishes feeling small in a wider perspective from feeling that one’s life matters less.
papers.notes: Free link is the in-press manuscript hosted by a Duke University lab.

papers.title: Prevalent mesenchymal drift in aging and disease is reversed by partial reprogramming
papers.authors: Jinlong Y. Lu, William B. Tu, Ronghui Li et al.
papers.headline: Partial epigenetic reprogramming reverses age-related cell identity drift before dedifferentiation
papers.summary: Analyzing gene expression across over 40 human tissues and 20 diseases, researchers identified widespread mesenchymal drift, a progressive shift of specialized cells toward fibrotic support-cell gene programs linked to higher mortality. Brief exposure to Yamanaka reprogramming factors—proteins that reset epigenetic marks—reversed this drift in human cells and mice without erasing cell identity.
papers.why_it_matters: Identifies a shared tissue-aging signature in humans and shows how partial epigenetic reprogramming restores cellular gene programs preclinically.
papers.notes: Human multi-tissue transcriptomic analysis plus partial-reprogramming experiments in aged human fibroblasts; mouse results largely reanalyse earlier published data (Browder et al.). Not tested in humans. Electronic date 2025-08-14 (PMID 40816266); Crossref lists print issue 2025-10.

papers.title: Effectiveness of pranayama for mental disorders: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
papers.authors: Christian Mütze, Dietmar Mitzinger, Heidemarie Haller
papers.headline: Meta-analysis finds tentative, low-certainty symptom relief from yogic breathing in mental disorders
papers.summary: Six small randomized trials totaling 517 patients with PTSD, depression or mixed non-psychotic disorders were pooled. Pranayama (yogic breathing) modestly reduced overall symptom scores versus passive controls and matched standard care, with no significant effect on depression alone, while adverse events were reported more often with fast than slow breathing.
papers.why_it_matters: Offers a cautious clinical evidence summary for breath practices in mental disorders, highlighting high bias risk and fast-breathing safety concerns.
papers.notes: Four of the six included trials had high risk of bias, and the authors explicitly state pranayama should not replace standard therapies; published in Frontiers in Psychiatry.

papers.title: “Sun brings all things”: Sun and moon lore as biocultural knowledge on Aneityum island, Vanuatu
papers.authors: K. David Harrison, Neal Kelso, Dominik M. Ramík et al.
papers.headline: Sun and Moon stories guide everyday practices on Aneityum
papers.summary: Researchers documented how people on Aneityum Island in Vanuatu use Sun and Moon stories in farming, fishing, navigation, timekeeping, and ritual. The study describes how knowledge passed down orally helps residents respond to environmental patterns and how local efforts are keeping that knowledge in use.
papers.why_it_matters: It documents how astronomical observation, oral tradition, and environmental knowledge work together in a living Pacific tradition.

papers.title: Identification of proliferating neural progenitors in the adult human hippocampus
papers.authors: Ionut Dumitru, Marta Paterlini, Margherita Zamboni et al.
papers.headline: Dividing neural stem-like cells found in adult human hippocampus
papers.summary: Using single-nucleus RNA sequencing of human hippocampus tissue from birth to adulthood, plus a proliferation marker and machine learning, researchers identified dividing neural progenitor cells, which can give rise to new neurons, in adults. They were located in the dentate gyrus, a memory-related region.
papers.why_it_matters: It identifies dividing precursors that could generate neurons in adults, without showing whether they become mature, functional neurons.
papers.notes: Adult human neurogenesis remains debated. This study does not establish how often the precursor cells mature into functional neurons.

papers.title: Integrative Genomic, Transcriptomic and Epigenomic Analysis Reveals cis-regulatory Contributions to High-altitude Adaptation in Tibetan Pigs
papers.authors: Dingwang Lai, Xiaolu Qu, Zhen Wang et al.
papers.headline: Tibetan pigs adapted to altitude through changes in gene switches, including EPAS1
papers.summary: Comparing 484 pig genomes across altitudes, researchers found DNA regions under natural selection in Tibetan pigs, with the lung as the primary tissue. Combining packaged-DNA and gene-activity maps, they pinpointed variants in enhancers (DNA regulatory switches) near the oxygen-sensing gene EPAS1 and other loci, confirming in cell assays that they alter gene activity.
papers.why_it_matters: Shows in mammals that high-altitude adaptation tunes noncoding gene switches near EPAS1, the same oxygen-sensing gene selected in Tibetan humans.
papers.notes: Animal genomics and cell-assay study in pigs; Crossref lists issue date 2025-07-01 and online date 2025-07-11.

papers.title: Is criticality a unified setpoint of brain function?
papers.authors: Keith B. Hengen, Woodrow L. Shew
papers.headline: How researchers group spike times can change evidence for brain criticality
papers.summary: Criticality is a state poised between order and chaos that may help information processing. Reviewing 140 datasets published from 2003 to 2024, the authors found that the time intervals used to group neural spikes can explain one disagreement about whether bursts of activity show the expected patterns.
papers.why_it_matters: It argues that criticality may be a general organising principle of the brain as a complex system.
papers.notes: Peer-reviewed Viewpoint containing a meta-analysis by proponents. Criticality as a unifying principle remains contested.

papers.title: Human adaptation to high altitude: acclimatization and reversibility of haemodynamics
papers.authors: Yifan Xu, Qiaoyi Hua, Wu Chen et al.
papers.headline: Small Everest-region study finds altitude shifts blood-pressure gene activity, then resets
papers.summary: In a small cohort study, 21 healthy adults were tracked from Beijing to Tibet near Mount Everest and back. At altitude, heart rate and diastolic blood pressure rose while 350 blood genes in vessel-tone, oxidative-stress and carbonic-anhydrase pathways shifted; most cardiovascular and gene-activity measures returned near baseline within 3.5 months after descent.
papers.why_it_matters: Documents in a small human cohort how short-term high-altitude exposure alters circulation and blood gene activity, and reverses after descent.
papers.notes: Small observational cohort (n = 21); 48% of participants used supplemental oxygen and 14% used symptom medication at altitude, and blood RNA may not mirror internal organs.

papers.title: A quantum microtubule substrate of consciousness is experimentally supported and solves the binding and epiphenomenalism problems
papers.authors: Michael C. Wiest
papers.headline: A proponent reviews evidence for a quantum model of consciousness
papers.summary: The author reviews studies on how anaesthetics affect microtubules, protein tubes inside cells, and experiments reported to find quantum effects in microtubules. The paper argues that a shared quantum state of these structures could unify experience and give it a causal role, but the cited experiments do not establish that.
papers.why_it_matters: It lays out the evidence a proponent cites for a disputed hypothesis and shows where the interpretation goes beyond direct observation.
papers.notes: Strongly contested. This is a proponent’s interpretation of largely indirect evidence, not a demonstration that quantum effects underlie consciousness.

papers.title: Adversarial testing of global neuronal workspace and integrated information theories of consciousness
papers.authors: Cogitate Consortium
papers.headline: Head-to-head test of two leading consciousness theories challenges both
papers.summary: In a preregistered study, 256 people viewed images while researchers measured brain activity using three methods across groups. Some results matched predictions, but sustained synchronisation in the back of the brain did not appear as integrated information theory predicted, and the rapid prefrontal response predicted by global workspace theory was largely absent when images disappeared.
papers.why_it_matters: It tests specific predictions of two leading theories using experiments and interpretations agreed in advance by their proponents.
papers.notes: Interpretation remains debated; proponents of both theories have disputed how damaging the results are.

papers.title: Boltzmann brains and cognitive instability
papers.authors: Adam Elga
papers.headline: A philosopher revisits whether randomly formed observers undermine cosmological theories
papers.summary: Some theories suggest that chance could produce many conscious observers whose apparent memories were formed at random. The author asks whether believing such a theory must undermine trust in the evidence that supports it. A probability model built from an analogy about unreliable vision suggests the answer need not be yes.
papers.why_it_matters: The paper tests a philosophical reason for rejecting cosmological models that predict many randomly formed observers.
papers.notes: Contested in philosophy of physics: whether Boltzmann-brain-dominated theories remain empirically disconfirmed even if formally stable continues to be debated.

papers.title: Beyond cultural renaissance: Indigenous events as sites of resistance and resilience
papers.authors: Trudie Walters, Diane Ruwhiu
papers.headline: Media coverage of Matariki increasingly makes contemporary Māori issues visible
papers.summary: The authors analyzed 2020–2024 media coverage of Matariki, the Māori observance tied to the rising of the Pleiades star cluster. They found that coverage increasingly connected contemporary Māori concerns with colonization rather than treating the celebration only as a revival of tradition.
papers.why_it_matters: It examines how the public life of a living Māori star tradition relates to cultural continuity and visibility.
papers.notes: Qualitative study of media coverage.

papers.title: Functional connectomics spanning multiple areas of mouse visual cortex
papers.authors: The MICrONS Consortium
papers.headline: A cubic millimetre of mouse brain mapped for both wiring and activity
papers.summary: Researchers recorded the activity of about 75,000 neurons in an awake mouse's visual cortex, then imaged the same cubic millimetre with an electron microscope, reconstructing over 200,000 cells and 0.5 billion synapses. The open dataset links what neurons do with how they connect.
papers.why_it_matters: It lets researchers test how measured neural activity relates to the wiring of the same visual-cortex circuits.
papers.notes: This paper introduces the dataset and summarises findings explored in a set of companion papers.

papers.title: Invisible secularity: American theism beyond belief
papers.authors: David Voas
papers.headline: U.S. surveys reveal weakening belief beyond declines in religious affiliation
papers.summary: Voas analyzed two long-running U.S. surveys and found that younger generations were less confident in God’s existence and less likely to see God as important, even among religious affiliates. The paper argues that measures such as affiliation and attendance may understate changes in personal belief.
papers.why_it_matters: The study shows why changes in the strength and content of belief matter alongside changes in membership.

papers.title: The architecture of the human default mode network explored through cytoarchitecture, wiring and signal flow
papers.authors: Casey Paquola, Margaret Garber, Stefan Frässle et al.
papers.headline: The default mode network mixes cell types and balances signals across the cortex
papers.summary: The default mode network is a set of brain regions most active during rest and inward thought. Combining post-mortem tissue studies with brain imaging, researchers found it contains varied cell-layer types, has a core relatively insulated from sensory input, and uniquely balances its output across levels of sensory processing.
papers.why_it_matters: It provides an anatomical basis for investigating how this network may contribute to complex thought.
papers.notes: The author correction added a missing middle initial (doi:10.1038/s41593-025-01900-x); it did not change the findings. Signal-flow results come from models of imaging data.

papers.title: Parallel roads, solstice and sacred geography at the Gasco Site: a Chacoan ritual landscape
papers.authors: Robert S. Weiner, Richard A. Friedman, John R. Stein
papers.headline: Chacoan roads align with springs and the winter solstice sunrise
papers.summary: Using laser mapping and fieldwork, archaeologists found that the Gasco Road system south of Chaco Canyon extends farther than previously known. They documented alignments between springs and toward the winter solstice sunrise over Mount Taylor, which is sacred to contemporary Indigenous peoples.
papers.why_it_matters: It connects sky observation to the study of ancient construction and sacred geography in the U.S. Southwest.
papers.notes: The alignments are measurable; their ancient ritual meaning is an archaeological interpretation.

papers.title: The metabolic costs of cognition
papers.authors: Sharna D. Jamadar, Anna Behler, Hamish Deery et al.
papers.headline: How the energy-hungry human brain balances complex thinking against fuel costs
papers.summary: This review examines how the human brain balances complex behaviour against energy use. Humans favour complex behaviour and so have relatively high brain energy use, yet many thrifty processes still limit costs. The authors cover both baseline upkeep and task-related thinking, and how disrupted metabolism appears in neurocognitive diseases.
papers.why_it_matters: It frames the brain's high energy demand as a core design constraint shaping how this complex system computes.
papers.notes: Free copy is the authors' preprint on OSF.
